desc:
An m x n map starts as all water. The entry positions[k] = [r, c] turns the cell in row r, column c into land; if that cell is already land nothing changes.

An island is a maximal set of land cells connected through shared sides (up, down, left, right). Return an array whose k-th element is the number of cells of the largest island right after the k-th operation.

m = 3, n = 3
positions = [[0,0],[0,1],[2,2],[1,1],[2,1],[0,0]]

result = [1,2,2,3,5,5]

Adding (2,1) at step 5 joins the island {(0,0),(0,1),(1,1)} with the lone cell (2,2), giving 3 + 1 + 1 = 5 cells.
constraints: positions[k] = [r, c] with 0 ≤ r < m and 0 ≤ c < n
The same cell may appear more than once
hints: After one operation only a few islands can change. Is the largest size ever going to decrease?
A new land cell can merge at most four neighbouring islands, and merging only makes islands bigger.

Use union-find with a size per root. When a cell is added, union it with every land neighbour, then update a running maximum with the size of the resulting set. Repeated cells just repeat the current maximum.
editorial: Islands only grow and merge, so a union-find with sizes is a natural fit. Index each cell as r * n + c. For a new land cell, start with a set of size 1, then union it with each of its four neighbours that is already land, adding sizes at the root. After the unions, the island containing the new cell is the only island whose size changed, so the global maximum is max(previous_max, size[find(cell)]).

A cell that is already land must be skipped, otherwise its size would be double counted; in that case just repeat the previous maximum. Because the maximum never decreases we do not need to scan all islands. Total time is O(mn + k · α(mn)) for k operations.
